I have a telegram this morning from Vancouver to this effect:
Fifty coal miners from county Durham, England, stranded here owing to being induced to come here to work in Canadian collieries at Cumberland, Vancouver Island. Please bring matter up in House of Commons, and ask for information by Minister of Labour. Situation of men is serious, having given up homes and left wives and families there.
Has the hon. Minister of Labour received any information in regard to this?

My attention has not been directed to the matter. Of course, I understand that a strike has been going on in the island of Vancouver for some time. If the right hon. gentleman will send me a copy of the telegram, I shall be glad to look into the matter immediately.

Can the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) give me some information as to the supply of ice for the House of Commons and the departments? Does he get the ice under contract, and where does it come from? We have heard a good deal lately about polluted water, and we would 'be just as much in danger by using ice made from polluted water as by using polluted water itself. Does the hon. minister intend to ask for tenders for the supply of ice for next session, and will he designate the localities from which the ice is to come?

I understand there is a contract for ice, but the ice that is being used by members is not put into the water at all. It is put into a tank surrounding the water, so that- there is no danger so far as using the water about the buildings is concerned.	.

As the time has passed for putting questions on the Order Paper, I would like to ask my right hon. friend the Prime Minister a question which interests many of his supporters in the province of Quebec. As we may have an election before another session, it is very important to have an answer. Will he be good enough to tell the House whether the Naval Act of 1910 will be repealed, and, if so, when ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I may say, in answer to the very proper inquiry of my hon. friend, that we will give him information with regard to that well in advance of any election.

I would like to invite the attention of my hon. friend the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Perley) to a matter which is of great importance to the people of Canada, certainly to those engaged in the manufacture of pulp and paper in this country. I understand that in the tariff legislation now pending before Congress of the United States, it is proposed to insert a clause which will penalize the pulp manufacturers in most of the provinces of Canada to the extent of two dollars per ton, as against pulp manufacturers in any other country. The clause provides that, in the case of pulp manufactured in any province, in which there is any increased license fee or any restriction against export of either pulp, pulp wood or pulp paper, chemical pulp coming from such province shall be subject to a duty of two dollars a ton; whereas chemical pulp, which comes from other countries, and which enters so largely into competition with Canadian pulp, is allowed to come into the United States free of duty.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is taking a rather unfortunate time to bring up this subject, because there is nothing before the House. It could properly be brought up on the Supply Bill. I thought the hon. member was asking a question.

I thought the Orders of the Day were called. It was before proceeding to the Orders of the Day. This is a matter of public urgency, because, unless this Government takes some public action in a short time, it may be too late for effective action. Do not you think Mr. Speaker, that, as a matter of public urgency and with the consent of the House, I might bring it up at present?
Mr. TITRGEON.

I have no objection, and I think the House will have none, to the hon. member making any statement he desires.

I am much obliged to my right hon. friend. As I understand the ground upon which Congress is asked to act in the imposition of this duty, which is especially directed against Canadian pulp, as that certain provinces of Canada place restrictions upon the export of pulpwood. It seems to me that the matter is of such importance that the Government, if its attention were called to the matter, might feel it to be in the public interest to make representations at Washington which might lead to the abandonment of the proposed legislation. I think it might well be represented to the authorities at Washington that the export of pulpwood from private lands in Canada amount to at least 1,000,000 cords a year; and it seems to me it might fairly be urged that the mere fact that some of the provincial governments impose restrictions upon the export of pulpwood ought not to outweigh the advantage which the American pulp and paper manufacturers derive from, obtaining this most important supply of raw material.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman speaking of the total export or merely of the export from private lands?
The export from private lands.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: How much is exported from public lands? '

I do not know. But 1 think it might be fairly represented that, in view of the United States manufacturers getting from Canada such a large supply of raw material cut from private, lands, in regard to which there is no prohibition of export, the Congress of the United States might very well abandon the idea of imposing what cannot be regarded as otherwise than a penalty against the pulp manufacturers of Canada. I bring the matter to the attention of the Government in the hope that, by reason of the importance of the subject, they might think it worth

while to bring the matter in some way to the attention of the United States authorities. Of course there are several methods open to Canada. One would be to induce the different provincial governments to abandon the restriction which they place upon the exportation of pulpwood from Crown lands; another-and this would strike a vital blow at the pulp and paper manufacturers in the United States who get their supply from private lands in Canada -would be to impose an export duty on such material.

aware of the attitude of the United States Government toward the product of pulp mills as contrasted with their treatment of other countries in this respect.

Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved that the amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 211-Mr. Doherty-an Act to amend the Criminal Code, be read the second time and concurred in. He said: One rather important amendment was made to this Bill by the Senate. Hon. gentlemen will remember that in the Bill as it left the House there was a section with regard to seduction, and that clause 213 of the original Act was amended by providing that seduction by an employer of his female employees under twenty-one years of age and of a previously chaste character, was an offence, no matter what the employment was. That section was struck out by the Senate, and the present provision of the code that punishment for seduction shall be confined to employers in factories, mills, workshops, shops and stores, is allowed to stand. The proposed amendment to the Act as passed by this House extended the application of this provision of the code to all female employees, no matter in what class of employment they might be, thus making it applicable to domestic service. This amendment has been struck out by the Senate. Their Honours have also added a clause making it an offence for any person falsely to pretend to be a police constable. There was a minor amendment to sub-section 5 of section 4, and the word ' commissioner ' was struck out of line 23 of section 22, this word having been left in the Bill through a clerical error. With regard to the person from whom a certificate may be obtained for the purchase of revolvers, firearms and other weapons, the Senate have added police magistrates to the officials named in the Bill as it stands in this House. These are practically the only amendments made by the Senate to this Bill, of which the first named is the most important.
Motion agreed to, and amendments read the second time and concurred in.

Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved the third reading of Bill No. 249, to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the public service of the financial year ending the 31st of March, 1914.

On the first
day of this session the Government placed in the mouth of His Royal Highness the Governor General a statement to the effect that an emergency which existed which made it imperative that the naval forces of the Empire should be strengthened, and a measure was promised and accordingly introduced, with the stated purpose of strengthening the naval forces of the Empire. The Government did not succeed in convincing Parliament that there was such an emergency and as had been mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, nor did they convince the other branch of the legislature, where that measure did not pass. I think we are entitled to know what action the Government proposes to take as a consequence of the action of the Senate in this regard.

The question which the right hon.
gentleman has asked is one that deserves serious consideration and a plain answer. He declares that we have failed to obtain the consent of Parliament to the measure which was proposed by the Government and announced in the Speech from the Throne. We obtained the assent of this House of Commons, which represents the people; we did not obtain the assent of certain gentlemen in another Chamber who were merely an echo of the expressed intention of the right hon. leader of the Opposition. This was plainly demonstrated by the fact that hon. gentlemen on the other side, before the Bill left this House, asserted with emphasis, that it would be defeated in the Senate. Notwithstanding the protests of the right hon. gentleman, everyone knows, .and his own followers in the Senate have frankly stated, that but foT him that Bill would have been passed in the Senate. He has referred to the Senate as the upholder of democratic institutions and of the liberties of the people. I desire to say to him that according to his own express interpretation of the British North America Act he for years deliberately violated the constitution of this country] That is a strong statement to make, but I challenge the right hon. gentleman to deny it, and I will prove it out of his own mouth. Here is his language in 1896:
I charge, here against him and against
his party-	.
M. HAZEN.	.
Speaking of Sir Charles Tupper:
-that, in So fair as the Senate of Canada is concerned, they have all along for the last eighteen years disregarded the constitution of Canada in the nature of the appointments which they made to that branch of the legislature.
It was one of the well understood princi-pies at Confederation-and the hon. gentleman referred a moment ago to the debates of the Quebec convention-it was one of the well understood principles then, that if the Senate was not elective, and if it was to be appointed] by the Crown, then both political parties should be equally represented on the floor of] the Senate. The hon. gentleman has forgotten that rule in practice although it cannot have escaped his memory.
That was the right hon. gentleman's own interpretation of the constitution, that was bis conception of his duty, and I ask him to point to me one single instance from the day on which he came into power in 1896 until he left office in October, 1911, where he fulfilled his duty to the constitution as interpreted by him in the words I have just quoted. He cannot name one single instance. He charged Sir Charles Tupper with having violated the constitution. The right hon. gentleman's own words which I have quoted convict him with having himself violated the constitution and he cannot deny it. And then, having filled the Senate with members of his own party, he adopts a somewhat complacent and exultant tone now that he is able to dictate to this House through those gentlemen in such wise that he is enabled to defeat the desire and intention of the people of Canada as expressed through their representatives in Parliament, elected less than two years ago. So much for that part of the case.
The announcement by the Government of the United Kingdom that the taxpayers of the British Islands are to be called upon to pay for three dreadnoughts which - are to be laid down in the place of those that should have been furnished by Canada under the provisions of the Naval Aid Bill, is a matter for earnest and grave consideration. In the first place, that action of the British Government, according to my conception, shatters every argument and contention on the part of those who reiterated over and over again to this House that there was no condition of urgency. My right hon. friend was willing to give a guarantee of the peace of the world, he was willing to answer for it. The.re was no need of any further provision for the naval defence of the Empire; he was in the secrets of all the chancellories of the world, he was thoroughly aware of their beneficent intentions and he could answer to Canada and to the Empire that we might disarm, that no further preparation was necessary. This was mere irresponsible vapouring, as the right hon. gentleman must have known

himself. The answer to-day, a most convincing answer, is the action which the British Government have found it necessary to take by reason of the defeat of that Bill m the Senate at his dictation. The position in which the matter has been left by the unfortunate and ill-advised action of the Senate, following his advice, is intensely humiliating to the people of this Dominion.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It prevents Canada, at
the present time, from undertaking a duty which the vast majority of the people of this country are not only willing but eager to undertake in vindication of their sell-respect. The right hon. 'gentleman's unworthy and unpatriotic action prevents the people of Canada, for the time being, from undertaking that duty. However, it appears from the press despatch-I have no official communication on the subject-that the British Government have undertaken the duty which I think ought to have been discharged by Canada at this juncture, under the provisions of the Naval Aid Act.

It is a telegram from
' Windermere.'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know who the press corespondent is, and I am not answering for the accuracy of the despatch. It seems to have been accepted by the hon. gentleman's leader. For the time being, I am assuming that the terms of the despatch express with accuracy the announcement which has been made in the British House of Commons. The defeat of this measure by the Liberal majority in the Senate at the dictation of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, prevents us at present from arranging that the British Government shall proceed with the construction of these ships on behalf of Canada. Technically, the Parliament of Canada has refused this aid. In reality, this aid has been refused by a partisan majority in the Senate, at the dictation of the right hon. gentleman, a majority having no responsibility whatever to the people of Canada. But, in view of the fact that these pronosals were made by the Government of Canada upon information which they had received from the British Government through the Admiralty, which they regarded as disclosing' grave conditions, it may be possible in the future to make right that which has been made wrong at the present by the right hon. gentleman and his irresponsible friends in the other House. The construction of these ships is apparently to be proceeded with by the British Government. It is quite out of the question for us at the moment tonnake any advance or approach to the Imperial authorities under the condition which has been created by my right hon. friend because, technically, this measure has been rejected by the Parliament of Canada although, in reality, it has been defeated by- a few partisans in the Senate who do not represent in any -sense whatever the true desire and wish of the Canadian people. As the construction of these ships is to be proceeded with by the British Government, as they are apparently to be of the same character, the same strength and the same fighting value as those which we proposed, as they are to be employed for the same purpose, that of the common defence of this Empire, which we had in mind, it is the firm intention and determination of this Government, if it remains, -as undoubtedly it will remain in power, to bring down, at a later date, a proposal for the acquisition or construction of three battleships, as was proposed in the Naval Aid Bill of 1912. In that way, before the completion of these ships, we hope and expect to be in a position to say to the British Government: Canada is prepared to do now what the unworthy action of a partisan majority in the Senate prevented her from doing before; Canada will take over -and pay for and acquire these ships and will place them at the disposal of His Majesty the King for the common defence of the great Empire of which Canada forms a part.

Mr. Speaker, I thought any right hon. friend certainly did his very best to be severe towards the Canadian Senate, he must be the first to admit that his efforts in that direction have fallen far short of the performances of the press which supports him. The language he has used does not compare at all with the language of the ministerial press. To read the ministerial press, one would suppose that the Senate had committed some great error, almost akin to a crime. Sir, the truth is that the Senate has done nothing but defend the rights of the Canadian people. If I may follow my right hon. friend's line of argument, I may say that the Senate has done nothing but defend the rights of the people against a servile majority in the House of Commons. What have the Senate done? Have they done violence either to the law or to the constitution? Have they infringed upon the rights of this House? Have they infringed upon the rights of the people? Have they in any way sacrificed the rights of the people? What have they done? They have not rejected the Bill, as they might have done; they have simply said that they did not feel called upon to give it their assent, until it had been submitted to the judgment of the country. Sir, this contribution which was proposed by my right hon.
I friend, under the pretence of an emergency

which never existed, to meet the immediate need of the Empire, the Senate would have been well justified in throwing aside; but they would not take that course.
How do you know?

How do I
know? I know by the resolution placed upon the books. They did not say that they would not give their assent to this Bill. They simply said:
This House is not justified in giving its assent to this Bill until it is submitted to the judgment of the country.
This, Sir, is the resolution which my right hon. friend has the audacity to characterize as partisan. This is the resolution which my right hon. friend denounces to the Canadian people, when all it does is to say that the Canadian people shall pronounce upon the proposal of my right hon. friend.
My right hon. friend says that the Senate acted at my dictation. My right hon. friend mistakes my friends, and those whom I claim to be my followers in this Chamber or in the other Chamber. Canadian Liberals, whether they sit in the House of Commons or in the Senate, do not follow the dictation of anybody. I have seen in this House within the last three or four days instances of, after a caucus, hon. gentlemen supporting my right hon. friend being forced to give a vote that they did not want to give. Nothing of that kind has ever happened to any follower of mine.
My right Ron. friend says that the Senate should be reformed. It is up to him to reform it; he is in office now; he has power to do so. I have myself stated over and over again that the constitution of the Senate, nominative as it is, is not altogether satisfactory. The difficulty has always been to find a remedy. My right hon. friend will perhaps be as good as his word, the brave word he has given to-day, and let us have a Teform of the Senate. If he will, I shall be willing to give my assent. But, according to the views of my right hon. friend, the reform of the Senate is not to be based upon its constitution; it is to be according to the manner in which the members of the Senate exercise their power. If the Senators are good boys, if they consent to be simply recording machinery to register tlhe vote and the will of the majority on that side of the House, then their existence will be continued and maintained. They are a noble institution, if they do that; but if they have the audacity to have a will of their own, to exercise their judgment, and to exercise that judgment against the will of the majority of this House, down with them, and anathema on them. That is the basis upon which, apparently, the reform of the Senate is to Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
proceed. But let that pass; we shall come later on to that matter.
My right hon. friend has told us what will be his action: It is to be a repetition of the vote of the majority. My right hon. friend forgets that, according to all constitutional usage, the way to get out of a difficulty of this kind, when there is a divergence of opinion between one branch of the legislature and the other branch, is to appeal to the people. But my right hon. friend will not take that course. He says that he will repeat what he has done before: he will ask the House again to vote the $35,000,000 for the emergency. He may do that; I do not pretend to be a prophet; but I say to my right hon. friend that, according to all usages, he should do what the Senate invites him to do; appeal to the one body which is the master of us all, and the arbiters of our destining. He will not do so.
They are not masters of the Senate, and the Senate know it.

Not only according to constitutional usage, but according to his own words, this is what my right hon. friend was going to do. My right hon. friend has stated, not once, not twice, but a dozen times-in Montreal, in this House, and in Toronto-that if Parliament were against this policy, he would appeal from Parliament to the people. My right hon. friend will not, I am sure, deny that he has taken that position more than once. He will not deny that on the floor of this House, in Montreal, in Toronto, not three weeks ago, he stated that if Parliament were against him, did not approve of his policy, he would appeal to the people. But I understand that the new constitutional doctrine which is to prevail is this:	Parliament is no longer Parliament
as we have known it in former years; it is not composed of the House of Commons and the Senate; it is not composed of two branches of the legislature; Parliament is composed of the majority which sits in this House. Even we ourselves have only such power and such liberty as the majority is good enough to leave to us. That is Parliament according to the doctrine of my right hon. friend; but that is not the way I understand the constitution, nor is that the way in which the people understand the constitution. In confirmation of my view, I would quote what my right hon. friend said at Toronto. He spoke as follows:
In 1910 I moved in the House of Commons a resolution that Canada should place at the disposal of the Admiralty two battleships or armoured cruisers of the most powerful type. In November of the same year I declared that, if returned to power, we would seek directly from the British Government,

and especially from the Admiralty, definite information as to the needs of the Empire in naval defence and that, if satisfied of the need, we would appeal to Parliament, and if necessary to the people for immediate and effective aid. In the campaign of 1911, I made the same declaration in my opening speech in this province. No Government in Canada ever had a more specific and direct mandate for any purpose than that of the present Administration to perform this manifest duty.
This is the statement upon which my right hon. friend bases his case to-day. He says that he had a mandate from the electors in the election of 1911. This statement of my right hon. friend was made in the presence of the fact that he had by his side the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), which fact is an absolute negation of the proposition. The Conservative party in the election of 1911 were a unit upon one question-the question of reciprocity. It was the same in one province as in another province; whether in the East or in the West, they were all united against reciprocity; but on the navy, to tell us that my right hon. friend had a mandate from the electors is to put a severe strain upon our credulity. It is true that my right hon. friend stated in the elections of 1911 on the question of the navy, that we owed a debt to Great Britain. He was not satisfied with the manner in which we had performed our duty to the Empire by placing the Naval Act upon the statute-book, but he wanted to do something in favour of Great Britain. There, by his side, sits his hon. friend the Postmaster General, and his hon. friend stated that we owed no debt whatever to Great Britain. The hon. gentleman has the audacity-
Never.
Well, I will call upon my hon. friend to go and repeat in the county of Quebec that he never said that.
I never said that.

But we have more: we know that when the hon. Postmaster General went to Quebec county for his re-election he stated that he had obtained from the Prime Minister a pledge that upon any naval expenditure he would have a plebiscite. Where is the plebiscite, and where is the mandate of the people for this expenditure of $35,000,000 ? While my right hon. friend, in the election of 1911, was preaching that we owed a debt to Great Britain, his supporters in Quebec -and I see one sitting behind him in this House-were paying for the circulation of Le Devoir, and the apostles of Nationalism were preaching every day that we owed absolutely nothing to Great Britain, and that they were against naval expenditure
in any kind of form. I see in icy presence a gentleman who paid for the circulation of Le Devoir, and who will r )t deny it,
I am sure.
But we have more than thal, We have the Conservative party and the Conservative leader in the province of Quebec not only circulating Le Devoir, which, if it was not treason, was perilously near treason, but we have also pledges from Conservative members to the effect that they would not consent to any naval expenditure whatever. Time brings its revenge. We know the methods-not all of the methods, but some of them-by which the Conservative victory of 1911 was achieved. We have the edifying spectacle of the same men, who in Ontario were preaching loyalty, paying out of their own funds for the circulation of an organ which was preaching something very nearly akin to disloyalty. We have the declaration of Mr. Bourassa that he was cheek by jowl with the Conservative leaders in Quebec who were arrayed against the Government of that day. The charge was made in the province of Ontario against the former Government that they were disloyal, while in the province of Quebec it was charged that they were too loyal because they wanted to spend money for the defence of Great Britain. Mr. Bourassa further says that he has the pledges of men in this House who were elected to support no navy whatever. He says amongst other things that he received a letter enclosing the following telegram:
Mattawa, September 8, 1911.
Chaa. McCrea, Sudbury,-I am certainly opposed to the reciprocity pact and t'he naval policy of the Government, and will support a request for repeal of naval policy and a referendum to the people, no matter who is Premier.
(Sgd.) Geo. Gordon.
Mr. Gordon was the gentleman who formerly represented the district of Nipis-sing in this House. There was another telegram to the following effect:
Chas. McCrea, Sudbury, Ont.-I am on-posed to the reciprocity pact. I am opposed to the naval policy of the Liberal Government. I will support a request for repeal of same and a referendum to the people on the naval question, no matter who is Premier.
(Sgd.) W. R. Smyth.
This telegram is signed by the name of a gentleman who occupies a seat in this House, and with whom I have always had the best of relations-the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Smyth). He has stated that he did not write that telegram, and, of course, I accept his word. It is up to my hon. friend to say whether it was signed by him or somebody else in his name. That is the condition with which we are now faced; and, to tell us under such circumstances that the Government

had a mandate from the electors, is an insult to the intelligence of the people of Canada.
My right hon. friend -went a little further at Toronto, taking occasion to add a word or two to what he had previously said; and this is significant in view of the statement he made to-day. He stated at Toronto that there was an emergency. An emergency! Does my right hon. friend pretend at this late date that there is an emergency F Will my right hon, friend tell this House that if there had been an emergency he would have been satisfied, and the Canadian people would have been satisfied, to send three empty ships to Great Britain ? If there had been an emergency, it would not have been three empty ships that would have been sent, but thousands of our young men would have risen to offer their services to Great Britain. If there had been an emergency, from the shop, the farm, the lumber camp, the mining pit, our young men would have come forward by the thousands asking to be sent forward to take their places in the firing line. My right hon. friend in Toronto the other day, accused me of being a separatist. Let me tell him that I know the people of this country as well as, and perhaps better than, he does. 'Whenever there is an emergency the people will rise, as they did in 1899, to offer not only ships and money, but the service of their bodies, and to put themselves in the front ranks in order to take their share in the fray. *
But there is no emergency whatever, and my right hon. friend has just given us the evidence that there is no emergency. He said, as we understood from the memorandum statement of Mr. Churchill, that the present effective forces of Great Britain were not sufficient, that Great Britain could no longer carry the load alone, that the three ships that we were to give were to be in excess of the number composing the British fleet, and that this $35,000,000 would not form part of the British naval expenditure. Now we know that this was not an emergency contribution, but a contribution for the regular naval programme of Great Britain. My right hon. friend has given the best proof possible that there was no emergency, and I thank him for his statement, because it shows that we were right from the first in believing that there was no emergency.
My right hon. friend did more at Toronto: he added to the fallacy of the emergency another fallacy just as fantastic and far more mischievous and dangerous. My right hon. friend stated at Toronto1 that a Canadian navy was a separatist navy.

Hear, hear.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER.

Sir, I am not prepared-yes, I am prepared-for this statement. It is quite in keeping with the career of the Conservative party; it has been their stock argument for sixty, seventy, eighty years past. There never was a reform put upon the statute-book by the Liberal party-
Oh, oh.

-but it was charged with disloyalty by the Conservative party. It is admitted that the basis of the British Empire to-day is the selfgoverning power given to the colonies some seventy years ago. Yet it is a matter of history that the reformers of that day, Baldwin and Lafontaine and their compeers, were denounced as traitors, while the Tories of that day saw imminent separation in the very idea of self-government. I am quite sure, if my hon. friend had lived in those days, he would have been a Tory then, as he is now, and would have been against self-government as he is to-day against the autonomous organization of our naval expenses. In regard to that, it is sufficient to quote against my right hon. friend in Toronto, my right hon. friend on the floor of the House of Commons. I have his opinions here upon the navy. This is what he said on the 12th of January, 1910, when I introduced the Naval Bill:
Then, it has been argued that the creation of a so-called Canadian navy will have a tendency towards the separation of this great Dominion from the Empire. I do not see that it has such a tendency more than the organization of a militia force.
This is the answer which I have to give to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. I know quite well that their answer will be that the policy of a Canadian navy is a separatist policy. My right hon. friend will try to arouse the prejudices of the people in Ontario; his confreres will endeavour to arouse the prejudices of the people in Quebec. We are accustomed to that practice. We have fought it before; we shall fight it agin. No amount of argument will convince the people that it is a separatist policy-no,t even when it comes from the mouth of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), who has tried and failed, and will fail again. He says that a Canadian navy means disloyalty. That means' that Sir John Macdonald and Sir George Cartier, the fathers of Confederation, who first were in favour of the principle of a Canadian navy, were disloyal. Our policy is a Canadian navy. We desire to help the British Empire by taking our share in building up a Canadian navy. We wish to have the navy manned and equipped in Canada, On that question we have taken our stand.

Upon it we stand to-day, and I invite my hon. friend to give us an opportunity oE putting it before the people.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend, referring to
the action of the Senate, stated that the members of the Senate did not follow the dictation of anyone. I say that the Canadian Senate is a body not responsible to the Canadian people, or they would not have dared to reject this measure passed by this House, and approved by this country and the Empire at large. I say that the constitution of the Senate is not in keeping with the principles of British representative government; and the time will come, if we are to have action such as this on the part of that body, that their constitution must be changed and brought into accord with the principles of constitutional government in the Empire. My right hon. friend has stated that the members of the Senate were not dictated to. Will he deny that they have followed his lead in this matter? How shall we account for the action of Sir George Boss, leader of the Senate, on this question?
Because he is a great Imperialist.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How shall we account for the action of Sir George Ross, at variance with his public utterances of a lifetime on this question?
Never.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Sir George Ross, for years past, by his public utterances has been in favour of a policy such as was submitted to this House by this Government.

What kind of a
policy is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The only remark I desire
to make in regard to his actions in this matter, the course he has chosen to pursue, is to call attention to the verses of the American poet Whittier-
Not an American poet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-with regard to Daniel
Webster, the great apostate, in which he calls him Ichabod, and says: ' Walk backward with averted gaze and hide the shame.
Can the hon. gentleman give one instance in which Sir George Ross ever gave an opinion in favour of the naval policy of Mr. Borden or against a Canadian navy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will not allow my hon.
friend to interrupt my speech. I make the assertion, without fear of contradiction, that the whole course of the public life of Sir George Ross upon this question, his utterances before Canadian clubs and in other
places, are absolutely at variance with the action he has taken.

I rise to a point of
order. The rules of this House say that no hon. member shall use offensive words against either House or against a member. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the language which my hon. friend has used with regard to Sir George Ross, a member of the Senate, is disrespectful and offensive language and not such as ought to be used towards a member of the other House. I am sure that, if a member of the Senate were to use such language regarding a member of this House, he would be promptly called to order. I think that you, Sir, will agree with me that the hon. the Minister of Finance ought to withdraw that expression.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What expression?

My hon. friend knows
perfectly well what it was. The expression was to the effect that the hon. gentleman ought to hide his shame. I think it was entirely disrespectful, contrary to the rules of the House, and contrary to those rules of courtesy which ought to govern the treatment of hon. members of this House towards the other Chamber, as well as hon. members of the other Chamber towards members of this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In regard to the point of order raised by my hon. friend, he has been unable to put his finger on a single word used by the hon. Minister of Finance that can be construed as improper language to be used in reference to a gentleman in the other Chamber. I submit, before my hon. friend asks that that statement shall be ruled out of order, or shall be withdrawn, that my hon. friend is bound, in fairness to this House and under the rules of this House, to state what the objectionable language is which he says should be withdrawn and ruled out of order.
The expression was that Sir George Ross ought to hide his face.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member has stated the point of order fully, but in my judgment it is not well taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With further reference to the remarks of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) as to members of the Senate not being dictated to by others and by himself, it is a matter of common knowledge in this House; it is a matter on which I have absolute information that Some members of the Senate, who were in favour of this Bill as it passed this House and went to the Senate, absented themselves, when the vote was taken, out of consideration for their party loyalty to my hon. friend. The people of this country

cannot be made for one moment to believe that the vote of the Senate upon this question represented the convictions of the majority of the Senate, constituted as it is. It was party loyalty to my right hon. friend that dictated the action of the Senate. He has spoken with regard to the naval question. What is the position of that question in Canada to-day? For thirty years, ever since the conference of the 'eighties, this matter of naval defence has been the subject of more or less discussion and has claimed more or less attention in the different parts of the Empire. For years we in Canada have been talking about our duty to the Empire and of what we should do to take our part in the national defence. And, up to the time when the Prime Minister brought in his Bill, no action had been taken that would have contributed in any measurable degree to the defence of the Empire, or even towards the defence of our own shores. Canadians have been known throughout the Empire as talkers on this question of naval defence. That has been the reproach of Canada-that	we have
talked and boasted of our loyalty, but have done nothing. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition will say that he introduced the Canadian Naval Act; but we all know that that navy was not intended to be a real navy.
Order.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend
will disclaim any such intention, I will withdraw what I have said in deference to his express statement; but, so far as his intention can be gathered from what was done, I say it would appear there was no intention on the part of those responsible for that legislation that there should be a real Canadian navy. Even when the right hon. gentleman in this House, in opposition to the naval programme brought down by the leader of the House, brought forward his plan for two fleet units, it was perfectly apparent to us on this side that there was division among his followers as to what should be done, and that the right hon. gentleman's real intention was to do substantially nothing. What did we do? Let us look at this matter fairly:	The
Prime Minister of this country last year went to headquarters on this subject; he consulted the Admiralty and he brought back one of the most significant documents ever laid on the table of this House. If that document did not represent a situation emergent and fraught with danger to tlhe Empire, then no language could be made to convey that idea. The leader of the Opposition takes a different view. But as between the opinion of that right hon. gentleman and the First Lord of the Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
Admiralty and the British Government on such a question, I hope he will pardon me if I elect to take the opinion of the Admiralty instead of his own. The right hon. leader of the Opposition lost the political chance of his lifetime.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have sc much appreciation of the political sagacity of the right hon. gentleman that it would not have surprised me in the least if he had stood up in this House, as I think it was his duty to have done, and supported this measure brought down by the Government. He had before him a state document of the utmost significance as to naval defence, disclosing a situation of grave danger. That being so, he owed it to his party, to the country, to the Empire, to rise in his place and give adherence to the policy brought down. But he chose to take a different course; and let us see the consequences that have flowed from his action. But before I deal with the consequences, let me tell the right hon. gentleman that, so far as one can gather'the expressions of. constituencies, of the press and of every utterance in this country that is entitled to consideration, it is manifest that the policy of the right hon. Prime Minister has met with the abundant and hearty support ot the Cana-adian people.
Now, in what position is this country placed through the action of the Senate?- as my right hon. friend says, the partisan majority in the Senate. It is a position of humiliation for this country in the eyes of the Empire. That is the first consequence flowing from the policy of the leader of the Opposition and the resultant action of the Senate majority. Canada is humiliated in the eyes of the Empire by reason of the fact that after a condition was diclosed by the Admiralty such as I have indicated, an emergent condition calling for action, Canada failed to respond. After all our professions, after all our talk-
On, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -and I include hon. gentlemen opposite in that, because they also have taken part in it; as a people we have boasted for years of our loyalty and of what we were about to do-I say that when a measure is brought down to give practical, effectual aid in this crisis of the Empire, the leader of the Opposition and the majority in the Senate commit an act of political vandalism, destroy this Bill-
[DOT] Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I say it is political vandalism. There should be no exultation in bringing about a merely negative result in this matter. It is easy to destroy. Any

man whose hand can wield a hammer can break a statue, no matter how finely that statue may be wrought; and so, the partisan majority in the Senate can destroy a measure such as this, a measure of the utmost consequence and necessarily promoting the strength, unity and solidarity of the Empire. This is precisely what has been done-a body blow has been struck at the unity of the Empire. Who are comforted by this action of the Senate? The enemies of Great Britain are comforted by it. And who are discomfiltted? The friends of Great Britain throughout the world; every part of the Empire is disappointed by this action. Let us not deceive ourselves as to what has been done- a body blow has been struck at the Imperial unity which professedly, we have all aimed to promote. There is no getting away from it. My own feeling with regard to the right hon. gentleman's action is one of sorrow. I feel that a measure designed for the benefit of the whole Empire has been thrown out and nullified for merely partisan consideration. My right hon. friend taJlks of an election-

Which right
hon. friend?
Sime hon. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I am sorry, Mr. Speaker,
if I am out of order; I merely wished to ask to which of the right hon. gentlemen the Minister of Finance referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To my right hon. friend
the leader of the Opposition. I say he talks about an election. Does he quite realize the condition of Canada at the present time? Does he realize the conditions of financial stringency which are world-wide? What assurance have we from my right hon. friend or from the majority in the Senate, that if an election were held next week, their action would not be the same partisan action as within the last few days? He does not want an election; he knows it would be a crime against the people of Canada at a time such as this to bring on an election. He knows that right well. He does not want an election, but he does want the idea to be conveyed to the people-because he has a subtle mind-that he does want an election.
My right hon. friend missed the opportunity of a lifetime in not standing up- and i am sure he would 'have had no difficulty in obtaining the support of his followers in doing so-and approving this policy brought down in pursuance of what we must regard as at least an implied request on the part of the British Government that Canada should do her duty in
the serious situation which has been disclosed. But he did not do it; he has cast the die, and my own opinion is that in the action he has taken he has placed himself beyond the pale of political favour in Canada for the future. Is the British Empire to suffer by reason of the calamity which has overtaken the legislation introduced by my right hon. friend? The United Kingdom and the people of the United Kingdom do not create a party issue with regard to the matter of naval defence. When a measure of naval defence is introduced into the British House of Commons, all political parties feel it incumbent upon themselves as patriots to give it their support. You do not hear Mr. Balfour assail Mr. Asquith when Mr. Asquith brings down a measure to increase the effective naval forces of the Empire. There is no partisanship there; it is all true patriotism, and if there is any unity and solidarity in the Empire, I say that when this Parliament received such a document as was laid on the table of the House, prepared by the Admiralty and the British Government, it was the plain duty of the Parliament of Canada and the representatives of the people there assembled to accede to the request therein made, and to do what this Government called for. The whole tone of the press abroad, who are capable of judging these matters, is that in this situation the course proposed is the only effectual action Canada can immediately take. Once you make the British Empire supreme at sea you can take your time for those other necessary things; time for the construction of your large dry-docks; time for the fortification of your harbours: time to consider what is the best course to adopt with a view to building up a navy, because the building up of a navy is a matter of years. In the meantime the one thing needful is to strengthen that Imperial fleet without which local navies would be as paper screens against foreign attack.
As I say, in Great Britain they do not quarrel over these matters. When Canada failed in her duty by reason of the action of the Senate, the question was instantly brought up in the British House of Commons. What about the statement of Mr. Churchill, which I have read in this House, that if Canada did not do her plain duty in accordance with the requirements of the situation as disclosed in the memorandum laid upon the table of this House, that duty would have to be discharged by the sacrifices of others? Those sacrifices are now about to be made, because Great Britain knows the situation; knows the importance of Imperial defence; knows the emergency that has been create 1 and which still exists; knows the conditions connected with the European international

situation as we in Canada do not and cannot begin to know them. The British authorities say: If we are to maintain the supremacy of the British fleet in order to secure the safety of our shores, our commerce and our Empire, then we must at once do what Canada has failed to do; we must anticipate our naval programme and lay down the keels of three ships, and the people' of the British Islands must make those sacrifices which the people of Can-and have been debarred from making through the action of the Canadian Senate. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister comes before the House to-day and says that we are temporarily debarred from action; temporarily debarred from doing what this Government desires to do, and what the people of Canada are desirous that this Government should do, and he says that as soon as we can we will repair the error that has been made. Providence is on our side.
We have the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend says he
has the people; that I deny. Providence is on our side, I say, and there will come a time when a majority will not throw out a measure of this kind. My right hon. friend says we will repair what has been done; we will put ourselves in such a position that Canada's action at present will have been only deferred action, and that Canada will fully discharge her duty as soon as this Parliament is in a position to take such steps as will bring that end to pass.

I cannot allow the declaration
made by the right hon. leader of the Opposition that I have said that we owe nothing to England pass unnoticed. The right hon. gentleman and his friends and back-benchers may go everywhere; they may refer to tne newspapers in which my speeches were correctly reported, and they will find that no such expression was ever reported as coming from my mouth. I have always believed that we in this country, especially the French-Canadians, owe a great deal to England, and I have never changed my opinion in this regard. I may tell him now that he has no right in the dying hours of the session to try to create all over Canada the impression that one of the members of this House nttered such a disloyal sentiment as that which 'he has attributed to me. Whilst I stand here for the principle of helping the British Empire, the Tight hon. gentleman tells this country that I am disloyal, whilst he, with all his professed loyalty, stands up and votes against the very thing that would help the Empire. He attributed to me words which I never uttered. I have no doubt that he did so in good faith; his newspapers have lied so much and he has read them so often that Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
perhaps he actually believes them to-day. But I tell him once for all that the assertion is not true, and with all his years in political life and with all the prestige which he has as the leader of a great political party, he has no right to place in my mouth words which I never uttered.
I am told to-day that I have made this, that and the other promise. These utterances come with bad grace from the hon. gentleman who has thought fit to break all the solemn pledges he has made from the beginning of his political life to the present time. I am told that I have broken a pledge. Where is the party and who is the leader of the party winch is known in this country as the party of broken pledges? It has been said that I have said certain things at certain times and that my opinions have changed. Perhaps some hon-. gentlemen may have the right to discuss that matter with me, but I see before me an hon. gentleman who at a most solemn moment in the history of this country, said:	We shall send no volunteers to
South Africa, and the following morning he turned a wonderful somersault, changing his opinion in twenty-four hours. Such are the men who tell me that I have changed my opinion. They have become very sanctimonious; they have become very virtuous indeed; and they look all around and say: Where shall we find a man who has broken some pledges? who would join the procession of promise breakers that they have been for the last fourteen years. It appears that at a given moment I have promised a plebiscite or better than a plebiscite. This is another newspaper lie that I am going to nail down now. I contended that on the Laurier naval law, this law being for a permanent policy should not go into effect or should not be proceeded upon except after the people had pronounced upon it by way of consultation, plebiscite, referendum or election. I have been true to my word. I never said that we would have a plebiscite or a popular consultation about an emergency or temporary policy. I never said that and consequently I am not breaking any pledges or any promises in standing here to-day with my right hon. friend and leader and the members of this House in order to fulfil what I consider a most solemn and sacred duty to the Empire of which we form a part. I say that even if I had said before, in the province of Quebec or anywhere, that we should not have a navy without a referendum, that after I had seen and heard what I saw and heard in the Mother Country last summer, it was my most sacred, bounden duty as a Canadian to come back here and to take the stand which I have taken, irrespective cf the consequences. This whole country has been told that we have been working

hand in hand with certain members of the Liberal party who have become Nationalists. That is a fact. But when I am called upon, as a member of the House of Commons and as a member of the Government, to take a stand on any public question, I shall not go and look back ten or fifteen years and ascertain what I said at that time, I will take the events of the day, the circumstances as they are disclosed to me, I shall exercice my judment and my liberty of action as I understand it.
Le Devoir! My right hon. friend says that he has found me in company with the gentlemen who write in Le Devoir. He was in their company before Le Devoir was started, they parted company with him at a certain moment but they have met now and they have joined company. But, Sir, those bad Nationalists, those men about whom my right hon. friend spoke a moment ago, they are at one with him, they agree with him now. They wanted the Senate to kill this Bill. So did my right hon. friend. They are hand in hand. If I was in the wrong in being with them at the moment when I thought they were right, my right hon. friend has taken my place with them now. If I committed a crime my right hon. friend, who has had much more experience than I, has thought fit to commit that crime and, forsooth, to stand up and say that I am a 'big criminal because I have done it and that he is a big man because he is doing it now. It is really amusing to hear our hon. friends on the other side of the House. They are anxious to go to the people. Anxious? Anxiety is no name for it. But do they want the people to be consulted on this subject? No. I am going to prove it to you right away. If you want to have the opinion of the people on this question and on this question alone, if you do not want the people of this country to be told that they should vote for a French-Canadian against an Orangeman like Borden
Shame, shame.

If you want the people of this country to meet the issue fairly and squarely, the way to attain this would be to leave this question out of politics and not to have an election over it. A motion for a referendum has been made in this House. The gentlemen have had a chance to discard politics on this question and to have the opinion of the people on it. When they were called upon to face this issue they said: Oh, no, no, no, we want an election. They have not yet realized that the people have voted against them, and they believe that if they could only get another chance they might get back to the treasury benches, that is all. The people of this country are no fools, the people-
They may be fooled, once, but not more than once.
My right hon. friend is sitting in a fool's paradise himself.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I think the hon. gentleman had no right to answer me in the way he did. I have said that the people were fooled once by these gentlemen and now if they are in power it is because the people were fooled in that way.
Order, order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
wants to raise a point of order let him state it. I do not think that what he has proposed is a point of order.

My hon. friend hardly understands the meaning of a fool's paradise or he would see that there is no injury to him in it. So far as I am concerned, when this question came up, I used my best judgment and when I hear people telling us here that, forsooth, we are not going to do our duty on account of the big thing which is in the salary of a Cabinet minister, which has not been increased for the last forty years and than which any man with ordinary brains can make more at his own profession, I say that this is all claptrap. It is all right for some hon. gentlemen to try and say that to the people, but there is nothing in it. Let me say before I resume my seat that our hon. friends on the other side of the House have a record and a record which is well worth looking into before they throw stones into their neighbours' gardens.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition told this House this morning that the Prime Minister had at his left the Postmaster General of Canada who is a 'disloyal man. Sir, for the last forty or fifty years in this country we have seen at every point the party now led by my right hon. friend take a stand before the public opposed to anything that looked like the militia or defence. The Militia Bill of Sir George Cartier and Sir John A. Macdonald was opposed by the leaders of the Liberal party, who went around from platform to platform in Quebec telling the people that it was a shame for the Canadians to arm or to have a militia to defend the country.

We have had a curious utterance from the hon. gentleman, who is a follower, not of the present Premier of this country, but of Mr. Armand Lavergne, in an attempt to justify himself before t/he people of Canada. I do not propose to follow him along the line which he adopted other than to quote a statement made with regard to himself by the chief of the Nationalist

party, who has told us some of the inside history of the pact 'between the Nationalists and the Tory party in 1911. This is what he says of my bon. friend (Mr. Pelletier).
Although the slimmest, Pelletier was the hardest to get through, not only because of his Nationalist tendencies, but because of his kindly dispositions to business-complicated business.

Who says
that?

Mr. Bourassa, the
chief of the Nationalist party, He goes on:
But because of his kindly dispositions to business-complicated business (witness the mail sacks and padlocks). Lavergne did his best to make him pass muster and he could do no less for the most ardent of his disciples.
My hon. friend who has execrated and abused the Liberal party for the last quarter of an hour, is known all over the province of Quebec as the man who declared that he was a supporter of my right hon. friend, the Prime Minister, who is trying to pose before the people of Ontario as the man who has always been loyal, a Tory who has never had anything to do with Nationalists. Where are we in regard to this 'matter? On December 5, the right hon. gentleman who leads this House, repeated the statement which he alleged he had made in 1910. If he had told us some of the other things which he said in 1910 we would never have had a naval debate or Bill in 1912. This is what he said in 1910, he was going to do:	He
proposed to find out certain things by going to the British Admiralty, and then he said he would appeal to Parliament for immediate and effective aid, and if Parliament did not give immediate and effective aid, he would appeal from Parliament to the people of the country. That was the pledged word of my right hon. friend, the troth that he pledged with the Canadian people on December 5, when he came to this House and asked it to pass the resolution which has been defeated. Is he going to keep his word? Is he going to stand before Canada and the Empire as the man who makes bold professions as to his intention to go before the people, or is he the man who will hereafter be remembered as having skulked and run away from the issue when Parliament put it up to him?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member is
using language that is scarcely in consonance with the dignity of the House. He has spoken of an hon. gentleman having skulked and run away. I do not think that is in order.

I shall proceed with my argument. The issue before this Parliament and before the people of this coun-Mr. MACDONALD.
try is whether the Prime Minister is going to make good his declaration of December 5, when he told us what he was going to do. What does he do? He proceeds to abuse the Senate, dodges' the issue, and fails to frankly answer my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. He talks about Senate reform in a general way, and puts up the Minister of Finance to abuse Sir George Ross. In passing, let me say that the long career, the splendid record-
Oh, oh.

-the devotion to everything which makes for the maintenance of the Empire expressed by the voice and pen of Sir George Ross, are a complete and absolute answer to these men who ally themselves with Nationalists one day, and shout loyalty from the housetops the next. You have never found Sir George Ross surrounded by questionable associates, or by men whose devotion to the Empire was the subject of criticism. Let me say, Sir, in regard to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, who talks about our leader, and Sir George Ross having lost the chance of a lifetime that that is the way the Minister of Finance looks at every public question. The Minister of Finance did not hesitate in 1911, when he saw a chance to leave his party and to make some political advancement, to desert all the principles he had ever held. The Minister of Finance who lectured this House to-day is on record as having declared that up to the announcement of the reciprocity pact he stood for all the principles of the Liberal party. He therefore stood for the naval policy of 1909, so that, Sir, he knows how to take a political chance when it means political advancement for himself. He is astounded to find that there are men in public life who are animated by principle, animated by devotion to sound ideas in regard to Empire preservation, and who are prepared to stand for them, even, if for the moment, they may be in the shade, with the absolute consciousness that time will vindicate them and that results will bring to fruition a proper policy and the only proper policy under which this Empire can be assisted. Sir, when these men talk about Downing Street, and instruct Canadian public men what to do do they realize that they are saying to the Canadian people that they cannot exercise their judgment, that they cannot exercise their Canadian intellect in regard to what is best for Canada and for the Empire. They must at all times be subservient to the line of thought that comes from Downing Street. God save Canada if Toronto is the embodiment of the patriotic ideas of this country. The Liberal party and our leaders stand for the idea of an Empire which can only

live by the certainty of the attainment and security of the rights of each individual part of it. We believe that Canada, Australia, South Africa and New Zealand have as much right in the Empire as the Mother Country. We believe that the Empire can never stand otherwise. The truth of that is being acknowledged, and it is being recognized that a man who is born in Canada has as much right to say what he believes to be the best for the Empire quite as well as the man who is born under the shadow of Westminster. We believe in the idea that a Canadian is as good as any other man in the British Empire. There is not a man on this side of the Speaker who, on this question has any doubts about the future. We follow the lines that our leader laid down years ago, of Empire maintenance and preservation. We know that the country will vindicate our position and we know that time will show that only along the line upon which Sir Wilfrid Laurier has gone can this Empire stand.
