speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The question of the hon. member is as follows:
Is it the intention of the Government to reimburse the depositors of the Farmers' Bank? If so, does the Government propose to act in like manner with the depositors of the Bank of St. Jean and of the Bank Ville Marie?
The answer is as follows: It appears from the report of the commissioner appointed to investigate the matter of the failure of the Farmers" Bank (a) That the issue of the certificate of the Treasury Board authorizing the bank to commence business, was procured by false and fraudulent representations on the part of the promoter and subsequent general manager of the bank, W. R. Travers, (b) That in the commissioner's opinion it was incumbent upon the Treasury Board before issuing its certificate, to have investigated certain charges made to the Department of Finance that the amount required by the Bank Act to be paid in respect of subscriptions, had not in fact been so paid, and (c) That if the true facts had been disclosed, the certificate of the Treasury Board would not have been given, and thus the bank under the management of Travers would not have been authorized to commence business.	_
The'case is of exceptional and indeed unique character, both with regard to the fraudulent means by which the certificate was procured and in respect of the results which followed, involving the ultimate loss of all moneys placed in the bank by the unfortunate depositors. The man who fraudulently procured the certificate in the name of the bank, was enabled to attract those deposits by the unwarranted assumption of powers in violation of plain statutory conditions. While the direct subsequent cause of the loss was the fraud and dishonesty of the bank's manager in the administration of its affairs, there is nevertheless a certain connection between that loss and the power and status with which he became invested upon the granting of the certificate. Having regard to these considerations, the Government consider that the depositors are entitled to a reasonable measure of relief, which will

be provided by legislation to be introduced at the next session of Parliament.
The case of the other banks mentioned, is in no wise similar, and the action which the Government propose to take in the case of the Farmers' Bank will afford no warrant or precedent for reimbursing their depositors.

I
ask to be allowed to take up a few moments of the time of the House to call attention to a matter of urgent importance. I would ask particularly that the acting Minister of the Interior should consider this subject. It goes without saying that the immigrants who come to this country under inducements that are held out by our agents are in a very important sense the wards of our Government. Especially are we in duty bound to see to it that in the case of young girls coming to this country no advantage is taken of them and no harm comes to them. I have information from people who are well informed on the subject which leads me to believe that more care should be taken to protect especially this class of immigrants. Some of the reports may be exaggerated, and for that reason I will not give the figures that have been given to me. But I am told that out of 1,400 young girls coming into this country, a large number are unaccounted for when their parties reach their destination. I would suggest to the Minister of the Interior that provision should be made on the train to look after these immigrants, for otherwise they may be led into difficulties by designing people. I had an instance brought to my attention by a gentleman who was personally aware of the facts. In one of our cities-I will not give the name-several of these women immigrants arrived at the station and were directed to go to a certain place where there was a refuge for them. The gentleman who gave me the facts, whose business it was to assist and look after ' these people under the direction of some society in the city, noticed at the station a young girl apparently loitering about. He spoke to her. He found that she was from Sweden and could not speak a word of English. She had a card directing her to a certain number of a certain street, and on the card was a written statement that her sister would meet her or call for her. The street had not a good name, and evidently the sister had not met the girl. So, this gentleman sent the girl in a cab to the address given, but told the driver not to leave her there until he found out the character of the place. And the place was found to he one not of desirable character by any means. This innocent girl did not know what was on the card, and the statement that she was to be met
i	

by her sister was evidently intended merely to deceive the authorities. There should be some provision on the trains throughout the country to see that these people come to no harm in their transit to their destinations in Canada. These people are wards of our Government, and we should feel our responsibility for their safety.

The hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) spoke to me personally on this subject, asking me if I would support him in bringing it to the attention of the House, which I am glad to do. I happen to know something about this matter, having made inquiries, being indirectly interested in the work that is carried on for the protection of these girls. It is appalling to find the offenses that are committed every day which ought to command the attention of this House and action on the part of the minister, as I fancy they would if the minister felt that in any extraordinary efforts he put forth he would have the support and endorsation of the House. And I fancy there is not the slightest inclination on the part of any hon. member to be stingy in providing the means to superintend this immigration, especially in large cities. I am informed that it was only a short time ago discovered, that in the Union Station, Toronto, the young fellows employed as red caps actually engaged in assaulting the young girls coming from the Old Country. This sort of thing is going on to an alarming extent all over the country. Some people say these reports are exaggerated. The extent of the evil may be exaggerated, but there is no doubt that it is of an appalling character.

While I hope the conditions are not as bad as my hon. friend from West Peterborough has indicated, yet I am sure that we all feel that any steps that can be taken for the protection of female immigrants should be taken. I think there will be no difference of opinion on that question throughout the House. I think it ought not to be a very difficult matter to attend to. It should only include bringing them into the country and getting them to the West, for when they reach the West it will be easy to provide each of them with the proper natural protector of a young girl.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The subject brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Dundas and the other members is one worthy of most serious consideration. As a matter of fact, during the past year, I have been in communication on many occasions with Colonel Sherwood, head of the Dominion Police, who has performed important duties in this regard and has had opportunity for giving it special attention,

in addition to the work carried on, as I understand, by the Department of Immigration. It is possible that sometimes the reports we get of these matters are a little exaggerated. A case was brought to my attention five or six months ago. It was supposed that two highly respectable girls from the United Kingdom had been led astray on coming to Canada. They had come out to take service in the household of a former member of this House, Mr. Ganong. He came to see me with regard to the matter, and we had the Dominion Police and other authorities making search for these girls all over the country. Eventually, it was discovered that they were in Montreal, where they had found more remunerative employment than they could get in Mr. Ganong's household, and were doing very well indeed. So we- must not believe that all girls who have been lost sight of have absolutely been led astray. But I do not doubt that there are evils in connection with this matter that ought to be redressed. I asked Colonel Sherwood to take it up and to make suggestions to myself and to the Minister of Justice. He has done so. His suggestions have been carried out, in the first place, by certain amendments to the Criminal Code, which have been assented to by the Senate without any limitation of these sections, as I understand. In addition to that, Colonel Sherwood thought that an additional appropriation of $10,000 would be necessary for him to carry on additional work which, in his judgment, would be necessary. In this matter I relied largely, indeed altogether, upon the report he made to me and to the Minister of Justice, as the result of his investigation. In the estimates which went through last night, there was one item in the supplementary estimates which, to the extent of $10,000 is to be at the disposal of Colonel Sherwood for this work. I can assure my hon. friend from Dundas, and other hon. members who have alluded to the subject, and all the members of the House, that so far as I am personally concerned, there is no effort that I will leave unmade to stop this evil. I regard it as the absolute duty of this Parliament, and especially of this Government, to put forth every effort to make offenses of this kind impossible so far as that can be done by legislation. The efforts we are making in that direction are, so far as we know, the best that can be made. I have spoken of prevention; I want to speak also of punishment. If any further amendment to the Criminal Code can be provided for the purpose of tracing and discovering those who make their livelihood by this means, and of punishing them as they ought, to be punished for their efforts to lead innocent girls astray, I am willing to pledge myself to this Parliament and to the people of this country, Mr. BORDEN.
so far ais my ability goes, to put such a measure through the House and to endeavour to obtain for it the consent of Parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
There can be no two opinions
among the members of this House concerning the importance of the problem of immigration. Our uninterrupted prosperity will depend very largely upon the continuous inflow of desirable immigrants; I am glad to say that immigration into Canada has been largely on the increase, and that the quality also is better than ever before. It seems to me, and I have thought so for a long time, that it is very desirable that more attention should be given to immigrants when they reach the shores of this country. I think our policy should be to guide rather than send newcomers to this country to their destinations. My attention was called a few months ago, as the head of the Department of Labour, to several employment agencies which were suspected of swindling immigrants at ports of entry.
I caused an inquiry to be made concerning the matter, and I found that the complaints were well founded. We found in Montreal that one employment agency had obtained from the immigrants in three months $10,000. They were in the habit of charging the men who applied to them for employment $15; they made arrangements with the railway companies whereby these immigrants were taken to certain portions of the country for a certain amount of money, and they were charging the immigrants a great deal more than they should. As a result of the report I received concerning these matters, I caused a set of regulations to be made under section 66 of the Immigration Act, whereby everyone who has any dealings with immigrants is obliged to take out a license and to record certain particulars concerning the man who seeks employment-where he comes from, who he leaves behind, where he is going to, and so on. Although these regulations have been in force only two weeks, several convictions have already been made against employment agents who have been treating the immigrants fraudulently, and they have been severely fined under the regulations. I think every possible step should be taken to provide that the immigrants when they reach this country should be well treated, cordially welcomed, and assisted and guided to their destinations, rather than that they should be allowed to leave the vessels at our great ocean ports by the hundreds of thousands, without anyone to look after them, and go to Montreal, Toronto and other cities in great numbers. We have in contemplation the erection of a large building in Toronto which will be a kind of temporary resting place for immi-

grants coming to that city before they are finally located. As I said at the beginning, I think we cannot give too much care to the immigrants who come to this country. It is desirable that "we should get as many as possible, and that they should be worthy additions to our population. It is important that the newcomer should get a good impression of the country when he first gets here, and I think we have to a certain extent been neglectful in this regard. I am anxious to do anything I can to remedy what I consider to have been negligence in respect of our treatment of immigrants in the past.

I
am sure everybody will believe that my hon. friend and the Government will do everything they -can along the line mentioned. Certain benevolent associations, having become cognizant of the condition of affairs which my hon. friend the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) has mentioned, have provided officials at the railway stations to meet the incoming trains and to endeavour to prevent such occurrences as have been mentioned. I would suggest that in order to meet the case spoken of by my hon. friend it will be necessary to employ women, as these benevolent associations have been doing. I do not think it is right that the benevolent associations should carry that burden; I think it is a burden which should be carried by the state.

I see that a congress has been convened in Europe to which various religious organizations of Montreal have sent delegates. I do not know what the other churches in Montreal are doing; I know they are doing a great deal to meet the contingency, but I may -say this on behalf of the Roman Catholic Church: The Archbishop of Montreal has organized a committee of priests and nuns to meet Catholic immigrants arriving at the port of Montreal, and I have heard great encomiums in respect of the work being done by the Archbishop of Montreal in that regard. I think the same thing is being done in Quebec on behalf of the Roman Catholic church there. The hon. Minister of the Interior has been kind enough to give Reverend Father Casgrain access to the public offices there in order to facilitate his work. I am bound to say that with regard to Catholic immigrants we do not receive complaints, because the clergy and nuns take charge of the young girls coming into this country at those cities. I think that if the various church organizations would adopt the same principle, we would hear less of the sad news which has been imparted to the House by the hon. member for Dundas to-day. On
the whole I think the suggestion made by my hon. friend is an excellent one, that public opinion should be aroused, and that we should do our best to protect the young girls who come from other countries into Canada.

I want to corroborate what the hon. gentleman has said in regard to this matter. It is very important, and should be given the most careful attention. The Minister of Labour has said that there is a large building at Toronto which is used to house the immigrants when they arrive at that city. Is there any such building in Montreal?
My hon. friend misunderstood me; I said that the erection of such a building was in contemplation. I understand that a similar building is in course of erection in Montreal.

I am glad to know that, because Montreal is the queen city of the Dominion. I am very glad to know that the hon. Minister of Labour is making provision to protect the immigrants who arrive in this country, but I would ask him not to forget Montreal.

I
would not have risen to say anything with regard to this matter except that the subject has touched upon the many complaints I have received during the last couple of months from the town of Stratford. Complaint has been made that the immigration service at Toronto, which largely contributes to supplying Ontario, is decidedly lacking in organization.' The principle employed there is not crystallized so as to deal specifically with men having certain trades or occupations and it frequently results that men with good trades .are sent to take up with farmers and farmers who know nothing about a trade are sent to take up in the city as common labourers or some such occupation. I have taken the opportunity of placing the matter before the present Minister of the Interior in the hope that a little more money would be applied towards the specific directions of tradesmen to proper places. It has become quite a serious matter in western Ontario, the getting of skilled labour, and I know personally many bright young mechanics from England who are to-day on the farms of western Canada because they were not directed as they came in to a place where they could serve and earn their wages at the trade to which they happened to have been brought up. With regard to the other matter, I endorse the sentiments of other speakers in connection with the female portion of immigrants and hope that the Government will back up the statements of the Prime Min-



ister and give specific attention to what has become a very alarming abuse in the country at large.

speechtext: I did not use any such words. My hon. friend has no right to impute motives to me. I want an election; I am sincere about it, and I would open the campaign in the city of Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend will always get a courteous reception in the city of Toronto. He is a brilliant orator, and he has a very interesting personality, but he is short on votes in the city of Toronto, and always will be so long as he continues to pursue the policy which he has pursued on the naval question.
Mr. MORPHY.
Referring to the financial condition of the country let me tell my hon. friend that the people of Canada are quite willing to risk any results so far as it will affect the finances of the country.
You have nothing to lose.

My hon. friend from Peterborough is quite correct, as he so frequently is. The Liberal party would not propose to risk any great amount of money in the election, and therefore so far as an election is concerned, they would have nothing to lose. But so far as the Conservative party is concerned, I have no doubt that they would risk a great deal.
I think my hon. friend (Mr. White) need have no fear as to an election disturbing the condition of financial affairs in the country. It is said by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House that the safety of the British Empire is greatly endangered because the Senate has declared that this Bill shall not pass until the people of the country have had an opportunity of expressing their opinion upon it. Well, Mr. Speaker, if hon. gentlemen are sincere, if they believe that it would be in the interest of the country and in the interest of the Empire that those three proposed dreadnoughts should be ordered at once on behalf of Canada, if they believe that they have the confidence of the people of this country, the matter can be quickly disposed of. Before hon. gentlemen leave Ottawa they could ask His Excellency the Administrator to dissolve Parliament, and an election could be brought on within four weeks of the date of dissolution. If they believe that the sentiment of the people of Canada is in favour of this alleged emergency proposal, of this thing which is the outgrowth of that unholy alliance between Conservatives and Nationalists; if they believe that the people of Canada favour such a proposition as that, it would be a matter of only five or six weeks before Parliament could be called together again, and if they could show to the Senate that they had a mandate from the people of this country for the vote of $35,000,000, and for the abandonment of the idea of a Canadian navy, they have in black and white in the resolution, which the Senate has passed, the strongest possible assurance which they could have, or could wish to have, that the Senate would without hesitation pass the Bill and enable them to send the money over to England.
What is there in the resolution of the Senate that conveys the slightest intimation that they would pass the Bill under such circumstances?

That is a very fair question, and I shall endeavour to answer it. The Senate has said that in their opinion it would not be desirable, and that they would not be justified in passing this Bill until the judgment of the country had been taken upon it.
Will the hon. member for St. John be content to tender his resignation if I tender mine, and thus Iftst the sentiment of eastern and western Canada ?
Now is your chance.

I will do better than that. If my hon. friend and I were to appeal to our respective constituencies, I do not imagine for a moment that the Senate would regard the result as a mandate from the Canadian people. But let us do what the Senate has said we ought to do, and that with which they will be satisfied. Let us ask the Government to dissolve Parliament, to take as quickly as possible the judgment of the people of this country, and then to come back and ask the Senate to act upon the judgment of the people.
None of you will come back.

Then my hon. friend ought not to be afraid. If we would not come back, then, in the judgment of my hon. friend, that would be the very best thing that could happen to the country, and, according to the judgment of my hon. friend, the sooner that could happen the better it would be for the country. Then why hesitate ? Why hesitate to do this splendid thing, as you say, for Canada and for the Empire. Why do you cheer the Minister of Finance when he says: Appeal to the country, not a bit of it; we will wait; we are plSying a waiting game; Providence is upon our side; vacancies will occur in the Senate; in the course of time, age and illness will get in their work?
_ Mr. WHITE: Do I understand that it is my hon. friend's interpretation of my words that Providence is on our side ? '
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am glad to hear it.

My hon. friend said that Providence was on his side. What does that mean ? It means that in the course of time Providence will bring illness and vacancies in the Senate, that the Government will have power to fill those vacancies, .and that by and by they will have a majority in the Senate which will not be a partisan majority. It will be a majority imbued with the sentiments which actuate the four gentlemen who were appointed to the Senate the other
day, a majority that will be able to do tardy justice to the Empire, and enable the Government to send over those ships to Great Britain. But that is a long time for the Empire to wait. It is asking the Mother Country to rest upon a very slender thread, because most of those gentlemen in the Senate are very strong and vigourous, and they may last longer than those of us in this House; so that for the passage of the Naval Bill we cannot rely on Providence. I am sorry to take up the time of the House when there are so many eloquent gentlemen hero who might better have spoken than myself; but I felt that I would not be justified in keeping my seat after the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White) who said that we could not think of going to the country, even to save the Empire, even although the Empire should be in danger and even when the enemies of Great Britain in all quarters of the globe are rejoicing by reason of the body blow the Senate has given to the naval proposition. Notwithstanding all that we could not think, says my hon. friend, of going to the country because of the present financial condition. Under whose administration has this present financial condition been brought about? How is it that with hundreds of thousands of immigrants coming into this country, year after year, with magnificent crops, with granaries overflowing, that never in twenty years has the financial condition of the country been so bad as it is to-day? Why, Sir, the explanation is easy. It is because we are importing such a vast quantity of goods into this country as compared with what we are exporting, it is because our merchants, our retail traders, and generally the people of the country, are paying into the treasury of Canada millions upon millions of dollars which have been taken out of their hard earnings and because we are sending abroad only about one-half of the goods which we are importing. That is one reason.
How would you correct it?

Get larger markets, call back the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) from the mission upon which he is engaged in seeking to negotiate a treaty with the distant, overseas dominion of Australia, which will be of comparatively little importance, and send him down to Washington to negotiate a permanent treaty under which the people of Canada will know that they can produce as much as they please, and, as far as natural products are concerned, there will be in the United States a market for their products. If reciprocity had been passed we would

not have seen the depression in this country which we see to-day.
Does the hon. gentleman realise that last year we imported more natural products from the United States than we exported to the United States?

What does that prove? That proves nothing at all. It proves that in certain sections of the country, where the circumstances suit our people best they can get certain products in from the United States, tropical fruits, among others, which our people are beginning to use in large quantities and many farm products cheaper than we can produce them at home while in other sections of the country, as my hon. friend ought to know from his observations of affairs in Canada, the United States will afford to our people a market which will be of enormous advantage. Look to the prairies of the West to-day, and this is one of the reasons why there is this depression in business which is affecting the East as well as the West; the price of wheat today in western Canada is ten cents per bushel less than it was when the Liberal party were turned out of office.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question?
Is the hon. gentleman aware-
One at a time, please.
Order.
I thin'k I saw my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) first.

I just want to understand the hon. gentleman's argument? Will he express the same degree of satisfaction with the verdict of the people on the naval question as he expressed at the verdict of the people on reciprocity?

I want to have one parting and friendly word with my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) before we go to our homes. It was not because my hon. friend was not without influence; it was not because he was without ability; it was not because he was obliged to say to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works that he was without influence and that he would have to yield to their powerful voice. My hon. friend was strong enough, big enough and occupied a sufficiently great position in this country to have warranted him in saying to his colleagues: I cannot do this thing that you ask of me. The late Government has left this tender there; it is deposited as a legacy for me to deal with; I have got to deal with it in the interests of my country, and I am going to ask you, my colleagues, to award the contract to this firm. Had that beeen done, we would have had to-day several war vessels under construction in this country. We would have had a Canadian navy well under way. We would have had not merely hundreds of men; we might have had two or three thousand men recruited from the Mother Country and making their homes here.

Honourable Gentlemen of the Senate: Gentlemen of the House of Commons:
In relieving you from further attendance in Parliament after a protracted session, I; thank you for the assiduity with which you have devoted yourselves to the important subjects that have been submitted for your consideration. The adhesion of Canada to the Treaty of of Commerce and Navigation between ' the United Kingdom and the Empire of Japan v if®? accomplished under conditions which should tend to promote friendly relations and increased commercial intercourse between the two countries.
Provision has been made for the establishment of a parcel post, the need for -which has been long felt; and it cannot be doubted that the facilities thus afforded will be greatly-appreciated throughout the Dominion.
The trade agreement between Canada and certain of the-West Indian colonies has now been brought into force, and it is confidently expected that trade and intercourse between: these portions of the Empire will be thereby stimulated and promoted.
The amendments made to the Criminal Code khould materially aid the necessary efforts to stamp out evils against which legislation has been recently directed in many! countries.
In wise recognition of the importance of transportation aid has bqen granted whidh should ensure the speedy completion of the transcontinental railways now under construction. The increasing volume of production and commerce is already taxing the capacity of existing transportation lines in all parts of Canada.
Among other important subjects which are receiving effective and well merited attention are the provision of further terminal elevators in the western provinces the equipment of national, ports on both the Atlantic and Pacific and _ the construction of dry docks of sufficient size to accommodate the largest ocean-going steamships.
The arrangement which has been consummated for a more speedy and more frequent mail service from Canadian ports to those of the Uniteti Kingdom has doubtless commended itself to your approval and will be hailed with satisfaction by the people Y.ou will be glad to know that the trade of Canada during the fiscal year just completed has largely surpassed that of any previous year. Immigration still flows to our shores in abundant measure, the revenues continue to expand and there is satisfactory evidence of development and progress in all parts of the Dominion.
Gentlemen of the House of Commons:
I thank you for the Liberal provision which you have made for the increasing neeWs of the public service.
Honourable Gentlemen of the Senate: Gentlemen of the House of Commons:
I trust that on your return to your homes you will find abundant evidence that the coming harvest will be bountiful, thus assuring for another year the prosperity which Canada happily enjoys.
